slides.title: Projection of planes
lines: Experiment 09
CAEG Lab · Semester I 2026–27
Himanshu Giria · PIET, Jaipur

slides.title: A plane is a flat surface
lines: Imagine a thin card. It has length and breadth. We neglect its thickness.
A square has four corners. Project each corner, then join corresponding views in order.
Today: true shape, edge view and the manual’s worked constructions.

slides.title: The point rules still apply
lines: Front view uses height above HP. Top view uses distance in front of VP.
a and a′ lie on the same projector perpendicular to XY.
Use a′b′c′d′ for the front view and abcd for the top view.

slides.title: True shape and edge view
lines: Look straight at a card: you see its true shape.
Look exactly along its surface: it appears as a line, called an edge view.
An inclined view usually appears shortened or distorted.

slides.title: Five basic positions
lines: Parallel to HP: true shape in TV, horizontal line in FV.
Parallel to VP: true shape in FV, horizontal line in TV.
Inclined to one plane and perpendicular to the other: an area view and an edge view.
Perpendicular to both: two vertical edge views.

slides.title: Surface parallel to HP
lines: All corners have the same height.
TV shows the true shape. FV becomes a horizontal line.
Turning the card within its own plane changes the outline orientation, not its inclination to HP.

slides.title: Surface parallel to VP
lines: All corners have the same distance from VP.
FV shows the true shape. TV becomes a horizontal line.
Teaching example: a 40 mm square, 20 mm in front of VP.

slides.title: Inclined to HP, perpendicular to VP
lines: FV is an edge view. Its angle to XY is the surface inclination to HP.
TV shows a shortened outline.
Teaching example: 40 mm square tilted 30° to HP about a side on HP.

slides.title: Inclined to VP, perpendicular to HP
lines: TV is an edge view. Its angle to XY is the surface inclination to VP.
FV shows a shortened outline.
Teaching example: 40 mm square at 30° to VP, with one side in VP.

slides.title: Perpendicular to both HP and VP
lines: The surface is parallel to the profile plane.
FV and TV are both straight lines perpendicular to XY.
A side view would show the true shape.

slides.title: The manual’s 40 mm square
lines: Surface parallel to HP and 20 mm above it. Draw projections for:

(a) A side parallel to VP.
(b) A side at 30° to VP.
(c) All sides equally inclined to VP.
The distance from VP is unspecified. Choose a convenient gap for the TV.

slides.title: Square (a), step 1: true-shape TV
lines: Draw XY. Leave space below it.
Draw a square abcd of side 40 mm with ad parallel to XY.
A side parallel to VP is parallel to XY in this true-shape top view.

slides.title: Square (a), step 2: the height line
lines: Project every corner upward, perpendicular to XY.
Draw a line parallel to XY, 20 mm above it.
The intersections give a′, b′, c′ and d′. Darken their common edge view.

slides.title: Square (b): the side turns 30°
lines: Draw the same 40 mm square in TV with ad at 30° to XY.
Project all four corners to the 20 mm height line.
FV stays horizontal. The surface remains parallel to HP.

slides.title: Square (c): equally inclined sides
lines: Draw the true-shape square with its sides at 45° to XY.
Project all corners to the same 20 mm height line.
Opposite corners b′ and d′ coincide at the centre of the FV.

slides.title: A side angle and a surface angle
lines: In the manual’s square (b), a side is 30° to VP.
The surface is still parallel to HP. Its inclination to HP is 0°.
A tilted side in a true-shape view does not by itself mean the surface has tilted.

slides.title: Inclined square: the construction
lines: Extra teaching example: a 40 mm square, one side on HP, surface 30° to HP and perpendicular to VP.
First draw its true-shape TV with the resting side perpendicular to XY.
Its initial FV lies on XY. Turn that edge view through 30°, keeping the resting side on XY.

slides.title: Inclined square: the new top view
lines: Draw projectors down from the inclined FV.
Transfer each corner’s original distance from VP using horizontal loci from the initial TV.
Join matching corners. The new TV is 34.64 mm wide and 40 mm deep.

slides.title: The manual’s pentagon extension
lines: Regular pentagon, side 30 mm. One side rests on HP.
The opposite vertex is 30 mm above HP. The resting side is 30° to VP.
First tilt the surface. Then turn the resulting TV to orient the resting side.

slides.title: Pentagon, step 1: the initial true shape
lines: Draw a regular pentagon of side 30 mm in TV. Keep ab perpendicular to XY.
Label a, b, c, d, e in order. d is opposite side ab.
Project its initial FV onto XY, since the temporary plane lies in HP.

slides.title: Pentagon, step 2: the 30 mm height
lines: In a new FV, keep a′ and b′ together on XY. Draw a horizontal locus 30 mm above XY.
With centre a′b′ and radius equal to the initial FV span, cut that locus at d′.
Join a′b′ to d′. Transfer c′ and e′ along this line using their original distances from a′b′.

slides.title: Pentagon, step 3: the tilted TV
lines: Project down from each point of the inclined FV.
From the initial TV, carry each corner’s depth horizontally to its new projector.
Join abcde. This shortened pentagon is the intermediate TV.

slides.title: Pentagon, step 4: the resting side angle
lines: Copy or rotate the entire intermediate TV until ab makes 30° with XY.
Keep every side and diagonal of this intermediate TV unchanged.
ab lies in HP, so its top view shows its true angle to VP.

slides.title: Pentagon, step 5: the final FV
lines: Project upward from the final TV.
For each named corner, transfer its height from the tilted FV with a horizontal locus.
Join a′b′c′d′e′a′. a′ and b′ lie on XY. d′ remains 30 mm above XY.

slides.title: Pentagon: construction checks
lines: Initial span from side ab to d = 46.17 mm. Use the measured span in the compass.
Surface tilt to HP ≈ 40.53°. Final resting side ab is 30° to XY in TV.
Final FV is an area view. After the last turn, the surface is inclined to both reference planes.

slides.title: Traces of a plane
lines: Extend the surface when necessary. Its intersection with HP is the horizontal trace, HT.
Its intersection with VP is the vertical trace, VT.
A plane trace is a line. A line trace, studied in Experiment 8, is a point.
A plane parallel to and separate from HP has no finite HT.

slides.title: Practice before checking
lines: 1. A 30 mm square is parallel to HP, 15 mm above it, with one side parallel to VP. Draw both views.
2. Repeat with all sides equally inclined to VP.
3. A 40 mm square rests on HP on a side perpendicular to VP. Its surface is 60° to HP. Draw its views.

slides.title: Practice answers
lines: 1. TV is a 30 mm square. FV is a 30 mm horizontal line, 15 mm above XY.
2. TV sides are 45° to XY. FV span is 42.43 mm, still 15 mm above XY.
3. FV is a 40 mm edge view at 60°. TV is 20 mm by 40 mm. Highest corners are 34.64 mm above HP.

slides.title: Quick viva
lines: When does TV show true shape? When the surface is parallel to HP.
When does FV become an edge view? When the surface is perpendicular to VP.
Can both views be edge views? Yes, for a surface perpendicular to both HP and VP.
Does a 30° side angle always mean a 30° surface angle? No.

slides.title: Your drawing record
lines: Write the aim and given data. Add the weekly title block.
Keep projectors and transfer loci thin. Darken only the completed views.
Label every corner, including coincident points. Add the specified dimensions and angles.
Sources: official syllabus Chapter IX and Lab Manual Experiment 9, pp. 63–69. Additional teaching examples are labelled.
